source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4

main.t: The head-shaped bone in the centre of the wrist, third in the second row of carpal bones (capitate).

simpler.t: The capitate is the wrist bone in the middle of your wrist.

deeper.t: It mainly meets the third metacarpal, the palm bone of the middle finger.

facts.t: It is the third bone of the distal row, counting from the thumb side.
Above it are the scaphoid and lunate.
The trapezoid is on its thumb side and the hamate on the other; below it is mainly the third metacarpal.

simpler.t: It sits in the centre of the wrist, in line with your middle finger.

deeper.t: It is the largest of the carpal bones.

items.name: Rounded head
items.t: Its upper end is rounded, fitting a hollow formed by the scaphoid and lunate.
items.check: OpenStax gives its name and its joints with the scaphoid and lunate; the rounded head fitting their hollow is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

items.name: Surface for the third metacarpal
items.t: Its lower surface, at the carpometacarpal joint.

items.name: Side surfaces
items.t: It meets the trapezoid on the thumb side and the hamate on the other.

simpler.t: It is the central wrist bone, named for its head-like shape.

deeper.t: Two bones meet it above, one on each side, and the metacarpals below, mainly the third.

facts.t: Its central position lines it up with the third metacarpal and the middle finger.
It supports the third metacarpal, which is firmly anchored and does not move.
Its upper surface takes part in the midcarpal joint, which helps the wrist move.

simpler.t: It sits at the centre of the wrist and gives the middle finger’s palm bone a firm base.

items.name: Midcarpal joint
items.t: Its upper surface meets the scaphoid and lunate.

items.name: Third metacarpal
items.t: Its main joint below, at the carpometacarpal joint.

items.name: Trapezoid
items.t: Its neighbour on the thumb side.

items.name: Hamate
items.t: Lies beside it on the little-finger side.

items.name: Carpal tunnel
items.t: The carpal bones form its walls and floor.

simpler.t: It is surrounded by bones: the first row above, its neighbours beside it and the middle finger’s palm bone below.

facts.t: It forms by replacing a cartilage model with bone (endochondral ossification), like all limb bones except the clavicle.
Its single ossification centre appears first of the carpal bones, during the first year.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20). Gray’s 1918 (8.2) gives the first year, before the hamate (supporting only).

items.injury: Overuse of the tendons or a wrist injury makes the contents of the carpal tunnel swell.
items.damaged: The nerve in the tunnel, whose walls and floor the carpal bones form.
items.cannotDo: Use the hand without pain, numbness or weakness (carpal tunnel syndrome).
items.why: The bony walls and floor and the tough roof cannot stretch, so swelling presses on the nerve.

items.injury: A violent fall onto the hand with the wrist bent far back.
items.damaged: The capitate and the rest of the hand dislocate backwards around the lunate (perilunate dislocation).
items.cannotDo: Move the wrist; the fingers may also be numb.
items.why: The lunate stays attached to the radius while the ligaments around it tear.

items.q: Explain why the second and third metacarpals give the hand a stable centre.
model: They are firmly anchored and immobile.
The third meets the central capitate; the second meets the trapezoid.
The fourth and fifth move a little, for gripping.
The first is separate, for free thumb movement.

items.q: Compare the capitate and the hamate.
model: Both are in the second row, towards the little-finger side.
The capitate is head-shaped and third from the thumb side.
The hamate is hooked and fourth.
The capitate meets mainly the third metacarpal; the hamate meets the fourth and fifth.

items.q: Predict the effect of a fall that dislocates the capitate backwards around the lunate.
model: The lunate stays attached to the radius.
The capitate and the hand move backwards behind it.
The wrist is deformed and cannot be moved.
The median nerve may be pressed on.

check.stem: Which metacarpal does the capitate mainly meet?
check.why: It meets primarily the third metacarpal.

check.stem: Which bones meet the upper surface of the capitate?
check.why: Its upper surface meets the scaphoid and lunate.
